toolchain.why: Cross-references the installed lockfile against the GitHub Advisory Database; no linter or type checker knows that a transitive dependency has a published CVE.

classes.title: Assertion weakened until the test passes
agentModes: Replaces a value equality check with toBeTruthy/toBeDefined after the real expectation fails
Swaps a concrete expected object for expect.any(...) or expect.anything() rather than fixing the producer
Keeps the test name unchanged so the diff reads as a passing test, not a lowered bar
classes.gapNotes: toBeDefined and toBeTruthy are legitimate against genuinely boolean or optional APIs, so this fires on honest tests too; it is a review prompt, not a verdict. It cannot see the opposite softening — an assertion whose expected literal was edited to match the wrong actual value — because that shape is indistinguishable from a correct test. Nothing here detects an assertion moved inside an `if`; vitest/no-conditional-expect covers that instead. The one deterministic member of the set is the literal tautology — expect(true).toBe(true), and its numeric spelling expect(1).toBe(1) — which is matched by a back-reference, so only a literal compared against the same literal fires; expect(true).toBe(false) is an always-FAILING assertion and is deliberately not this class.

evidence.source: Matcher names from the Vitest expect API; the class itself is behavioural and the regexes are reasoned, not tool-backed.

classes.title: Test body emptied instead of fixed
agentModes: Deletes the body of a failing test but leaves the it(...) shell so the file still looks covered
Replaces the body with a bare return or a TODO comment after failing to diagnose the failure
Reports the suite as green because an empty test passes
classes.gapNotes: Only catches the shell left behind. A test deleted outright leaves no source to match, which is what the `test-count-dropped` class in this edition reads instead — it counts `it(` in the text an edit replaced against the text it wrote. It also misses a body reduced to a single trivially true assertion such as expect(true).toBe(true) — the `softened-assertion` class in this edition matches that literal instead; vitest/expect-expect sees an assertion there and passes it. An empty beforeEach/afterEach hook is deliberately not matched, which means a suite gutted by moving its work into a now-empty hook slips through.

evidence.source: Rule vitest/expect-expect confirmed in the @vitest/eslint-plugin rule list.

classes.title: Focused test left in the suite
agentModes: Adds .only to iterate on one failure and never removes it, so CI silently runs one test
Uses describe.only around the file it is editing to shorten its own feedback loop
Declares the suite green from a run that executed a single case
classes.gapNotes: A focus applied dynamically — `const t = condition ? it.only : it;` or a runner flag such as `--testNamePattern` — produces no `.only` token and is invisible here. The regex is Vitest/Jest-shaped; a project on `node --test` focuses with `{ only: true }` options plus the `--test-only` flag, which this does not model. The Jasmine-era spellings `fit` and `fdescribe` are deliberately not matched, because `fit(` collides with ordinary identifiers such as a curve-fitting helper; a Jest repo that still uses them needs jest/no-focused-tests, which does cover them.

evidence.source: vitest/no-focused-tests listed in @vitest/eslint-plugin; Vitest CLI documents --allowOnly defaulting to !process.env.CI.

classes.title: Test skipped and left that way
agentModes: Marks a failing test .skip or .todo rather than diagnosing it, then reports the work complete
Renames it to xit/xdescribe, which reads as a legacy spelling and survives review
Adds a conditional skipIf whose condition is always true in CI
classes.gapNotes: The Jest/Jasmine spellings xit, xtest and xdescribe are not matched by regex — they are ordinary identifiers in a Vitest repo — so a Jest project must lean on jest/no-disabled-tests for those. Cannot distinguish a deliberate, documented quarantine from an abandoned one — a skip with an owner and an expiry is the same token as a skip added ten minutes ago to make CI green. It also does not fire on a test disabled by narrowing the runner's `include` glob or by adding the file to `exclude` in vitest.config.ts, which removes a whole file with no marker in the test source at all.

evidence.source: vitest/no-disabled-tests listed in @vitest/eslint-plugin; equivalent jest/no-disabled-tests confirmed in eslint-plugin-jest.

classes.title: Test commented out rather than removed or fixed
agentModes: Comments out a failing case to unblock itself, leaving it as apparent documentation
Wraps a whole describe block in a block comment while refactoring and never restores it
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic, because a comment that merely quotes a test call — a note showing the `it(` signature, or a code sample in a docblock — is reported the same as a real test commented out. It recognises the call shape only: a commented-out test written without its `it(`/`test(`/`describe(` line, for example a stranded `expect(...)` block whose header was deleted, is missed, and so is a suite disabled by wrapping it in a `/* … */` block, whose inner lines carry no `//`. Nothing here dates a suppression, so a test commented out this session and one commented out a year ago are reported identically.

evidence.source: vitest/no-commented-out-tests listed in @vitest/eslint-plugin; jest/no-commented-out-tests confirmed in eslint-plugin-jest.

classes.title: Test that asserts nothing
agentModes: Writes a test that only calls the function under test, so it passes unless the call throws
Moves the only expect into a conditional branch that never executes
Awaits a promise and never checks the resolved value, then counts the case as coverage
classes.gapNotes: No honest regex exists: proving a test asserts nothing needs the call graph, because the assertion is usually inside a helper such as `assertMigrated(db)`. expect-expect accepts a custom helper only if it is listed in the rule's assertFunctionNames option, so a project with wrapper assertions must configure that or live with false positives. None of these rules catch a test whose assertion runs but is tautological.

evidence.source: vitest/expect-expect, vitest/no-conditional-expect and vitest/no-standalone-expect all listed in @vitest/eslint-plugin.

classes.title: Exception caught and discarded
agentModes: Wraps a call it could not make work in try/catch with an empty body so the path stops failing
Attaches .catch(() => {}) to a rejected promise to clear an unhandled-rejection warning
Returns a default value from the catch block, converting a hard failure into silent wrong data
classes.gapNotes: A catch body containing only a comment is blanked to an empty block and will be flagged — that false positive is the price of the deterministic form, and no-empty behaves the same way unless the comment is allowed via allowEmptyCatch. The third pattern only lists literal default returns; `catch { return this.fallback; }` is equally a swallow and is not matched. Nothing here sees a catch that logs at debug level and then continues, which hides the failure just as effectively.

evidence.source: ESLint core rule no-empty and its allowEmptyCatch option are documented in the ESLint rules reference.

classes.title: Type widened to any to silence the checker
agentModes: Annotates a parameter or return as any once tsc rejects the real type
Casts an expression `as any` at the one call site the checker complains about
Changes a generic constraint to any rather than threading the type through
classes.gapNotes: Only sees the word `any`. A session that widens to `unknown` and then casts, uses `object`, `Function`, `{}` or an index signature of `Record<string, unknown>` gets the same escape with none of these tokens. The regex also fires on legitimate `any` in ambient declaration files and in third-party type shims, so .d.ts should usually be excluded from the paths glob, and on a call to a function actually named `any` written in value position (`{ check: any(p, xs) }`), which is the one shape that keeps this from being literally exact. It says nothing about implicit any. tsc reports nothing here at any strictness — `strict` and `noImplicitAny` govern inferred any only, so an explicit `any` compiles clean and the linter is the only tool that objects.

evidence.source: @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any confirmed in the typescript-eslint rules index (typescript-eslint.io/rules).

classes.title: Type laundered through a double cast
agentModes: Writes `as unknown as T` once tsc rejects the direct cast, defeating the check entirely
Casts a partial test fixture to the full domain type so a mock compiles
Uses a non-null-plus-cast chain to make an optional field look required
classes.gapNotes: Matches the classic spelling only. The same laundering written across two statements — `const tmp: unknown = x; const y = tmp as T;` — has no adjacent `as unknown as` and is missed, and so is the equivalent via a helper such as `cast<T>(x)`. typescript-eslint has no rule that bans double casts outright (no-unnecessary-type-assertion targets a different shape), so there is no tool-rule detector to pair with this regex.

evidence.source: Regex is behavioural; deliberately no rule id claimed, because no confirmed typescript-eslint rule bans `as unknown as`.

classes.title: Non-null assertion used to silence a narrowing failure
agentModes: Appends ! to a possibly-undefined access instead of handling the undefined case
Adds ! after enabling noUncheckedIndexedAccess so array indexing compiles again
Chains !. through an optional object graph a caller can legitimately leave empty
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic because `!` is overloaded. The lookaround-free patterns avoid `!==`, `!=` and prefix negation by requiring a word, `]` or `)` immediately before the `!`, but `foo(a)!` and `foo(a) !== b` written without the space around the operator can still confuse it in dense expressions. A non-null assertion moved into a helper (`function must<T>(x: T | undefined): T`) has the identical effect and no `!` token. tsc contributes no detection at all: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is the flag that makes the `!` necessary in the first place, and it never reports the `!`.

evidence.source: @typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion confirmed in the typescript-eslint rules index (typescript-eslint.io/rules).

classes.title: Type error suppressed by comment
agentModes: Drops // @ts-ignore above the line tsc rejects rather than fixing the type
Adds // @ts-nocheck at the top of a file it could not make compile
Uses @ts-expect-error with no description, so the suppression carries no reason for the next reader
classes.gapNotes: The check needs the comment text, so it runs with comments intact and will also report an `@ts-ignore` written inside prose — a note explaining why one was removed reads exactly like the directive itself. `@ts-expect-error` is deliberately not matched: it fails the build once the underlying error is fixed, which makes it the honest form; ban-ts-comment reports it only when it carries no description, and a description of three characters satisfies the rule. Suppression achieved by excluding the file from tsconfig's include, or by turning the compiler flag down, leaves no directive in the source at all — see relaxed-tsconfig-strictness.

evidence.source: @typescript-eslint/ban-ts-comment confirmed in the typescript-eslint rules index, with the documented allow-with-description option value; the @ts-ignore, @ts-nocheck and @ts-expect-error directive spellings are from the TypeScript handbook.

classes.title: Lint suppressed for a whole file or line without a reason
agentModes: Puts /* eslint-disable */ at the top of a file to clear every remaining error at once
Disables the specific rule that was about to catch the shortcut it just took
Leaves the suppression in place after the underlying problem is fixed
classes.gapNotes: The check matches a file-wide `/* eslint-disable */` and an inline `eslint-disable-line` or `eslint-disable-next-line` written without a `--` reason. A directive that carries a reason is treated as clean, so a plausible but false reason passes, and a reason that was true when written stays clean forever after the underlying problem is fixed. Only ESLint's directive spelling is matched: `// biome-ignore lint/suspicious/noExplicitAny: reason` is a different syntax and is not covered. A directive naming a rule that was never going to fire is dead weight rather than a suppression, and this cannot tell the two apart; ESLint reports that through `--report-unused-disable-directives`, a CLI flag carried in this edition's lint wiring rather than a rule id, and reports nothing at all about a directive that is genuinely in use but unjustified. Disabling the rule in eslint.config.mjs instead of in the source is the sibling class lint-rule-turned-off.

evidence.source: ESLint CLI reference confirms --report-unused-disable-directives and --max-warnings; the reason-comment `--` convention is ESLint's documented directive-description syntax, which is what the second pattern keys on.

classes.title: Type-checker strictness turned down to make the build pass
agentModes: Flips "strict" or "strictNullChecks" to false after failing to fix the reported errors
Adds the failing file to tsconfig's exclude list so tsc stops looking at it
Turns on skipLibCheck plus allowJs without checkJs so a whole language surface stops being checked

fixtures.nearMiss:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2023",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "allowJs": true,

    "declaration": false,
    "sourceMap": false,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "noEmit": true
  },
  "include": ["src", "tests"]

classes.gapNotes: It sees a flag written as false but not a flag quietly deleted — removing "noUncheckedIndexedAccess" entirely has the same effect and leaves no token, which is the most common way this actually happens. It also cannot judge the exclude list: a new path in "exclude" may be a legitimate build split or may be the file that would not compile. Detection is per-file, so a strict base config softened in an extending tsconfig.build.json is only caught if that file is in the paths glob, and strictness inherited from an "extends" package is never read at all. tsc contributes nothing: a tsconfig whose strictness has been turned down is exactly the state in which the type checker reports nothing, so it cannot detect its own relaxation.

evidence.source: All flag names verified against the TypeScript TSConfig reference (typescriptlang.org/tsconfig); suppressImplicitAnyIndexErrors is included as a legacy escape hatch and is a deprecated option, so it appears only in older configs.

classes.title: Lint rule disabled in config instead of obeyed
agentModes: Sets the offending rule to 'off' in eslint.config.mjs rather than changing the code
Adds the file it is editing to globalIgnores so the linter stops visiting it
Downgrades an error to 'warn' knowing the CI line only fails on errors
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic, because turning a core rule off is sometimes mandatory: `'no-unused-vars': 'off'` beside `'@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars': 'error'` is the documented pairing for the TypeScript replacements, and it reads the same as a rule switched off to dodge a finding. `'warn'` is matched because this edition's CI line fails on errors only, so a repo running `--max-warnings 0` will see a report where there is no defect. The config is read as text, so a severity computed at load time — spread from a shared object, or keyed off an environment variable — carries no `off` token and is missed. It also cannot see the two quietest forms of the same move: a rule dropped by swapping a `strictTypeChecked` extends for `recommended`, which leaves no token anywhere, and a file added to `ignores` or `globalIgnores`, which is indistinguishable from the `dist/**` entry every config legitimately carries. No ESLint rule reports a config that disables rules, so nothing in the toolchain backs this up; that needs a config-aware check which loads the resolved config and diffs severities against a baseline.

evidence.source: ESLint flat-config file names and severity values ('off' | 0 | 'warn' | 'error') from the ESLint configuration-files reference; Biome's biome.json carries the same string severities.

classes.title: Promise never awaited or handled
agentModes: Drops the await when converting a function to synchronous to make a signature line up
Calls an async function inside forEach, so the caller returns before any of the work finishes
Passes an async callback where a void-returning one is expected, discarding the rejection
classes.gapNotes: No check-driver detector, and honestly so: deciding whether an expression is thenable needs the type of the callee, which a regex over blanked source cannot know — `save(x);` is a floating promise or an ordinary void call depending entirely on save's return type. These rules require type-aware linting (parserOptions.projectService), so they are silent in a project that lints without a tsconfig, and they do not apply to plain .js files outside the TypeScript program.

evidence.source: no-floating-promises, no-misused-promises and await-thenable all confirmed in the typescript-eslint rules index; typed-linting setup confirmed on typescript-eslint.io.

classes.title: Import path or exported symbol that does not exist
agentModes: Invents a module specifier that matches the naming convention but no file
Imports a named export the package does not actually publish
Guesses a deep subpath import that the package's exports map does not expose
classes.gapNotes: No check-driver detector is possible: whether a specifier resolves is a question about the filesystem and the package's exports map, not about the text, and a regex that guessed would flag every legitimate import. import-x/no-unresolved needs configuring for path aliases or it produces false positives on every `@/…` import, and it does not evaluate package.json exports maps, so a deep subpath blocked by exports may resolve for the linter and fail at runtime. Dynamic `await import(variable)` is outside all four detectors, and so is a real module imported for a named export that does not exist on it.

evidence.source: import-x/no-unresolved and import-x/named confirmed in eslint-plugin-import-x; n/no-missing-import confirmed in eslint-plugin-n; module/moduleResolution values confirmed in the TSConfig reference.

classes.title: Package imported but never declared
agentModes: Imports a package it saw in another repo, relying on it being hoisted into node_modules transitively
Uses a devDependency from production source, so the import breaks on an install without dev deps
Adds the import without touching package.json, so the lockfile and the code disagree
classes.gapNotes: No check-driver detector: the regex would have to read package.json and cross-reference every specifier, which is resolution work, not pattern work. Both rules judge against the nearest package.json, so in a pnpm or yarn workspace a dependency declared only at the root is reported as extraneous in a leaf package unless the config accounts for it. Neither rule catches the reverse mistake — a declared dependency nobody imports — which needs a separate unused-dependency audit.

evidence.source: import-x/no-extraneous-dependencies confirmed in eslint-plugin-import-x; n/no-extraneous-import confirmed in eslint-plugin-n.

classes.title: Credential or token written into source
agentModes: Inlines a key it found in a log, a fixture or an error message to make an integration test run
Pastes a sample token from vendor documentation into production configuration
Replaces a failing env lookup with the literal value it was given during the session
classes.gapNotes: This detector runs with strings intact — it must, since the secret is the string — so it is the noisiest in the edition: a fixture password like 'correct-horse-battery' matches, and so does any long placeholder, which is why test and fixture paths usually need excluding by path. It only recognises the vendor prefixes listed; a bare 32-hex-character key assigned to a variable named `k` matches nothing, and neither does a credential split across two concatenated literals. It reads source files and package.json, so a secret written into a .env file, a Kubernetes manifest or a CI variable block is outside its paths, and a key already committed and then removed from the working tree is not found either. No lint rule in this edition's toolchain scans for secrets — security/detect-possible-timing-attacks is the nearest and reports something else entirely, the `==` comparison of a secret-named variable — so a dedicated scanner such as gitleaks belongs in CI beside this check.

evidence.source: Behavioural class; the credential prefixes are public vendor token formats and the regexes are reasoned. No rule id is claimed, because no rule in this edition's toolchain detects a hardcoded credential.

classes.title: Configuration value inlined instead of read
agentModes: Gives a required env var a literal default so the code runs in its own sandbox
Inlines a hostname, port or bucket name after the config lookup returned undefined
Hardcodes a path or timeout that the caller was supposed to supply
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic on all three patterns. The env-fallback pattern anchors on the opening quote of the fallback and says nothing about what the fallback is, so it cannot tell a sensible default such as a cache directory from a dangerous one such as a production endpoint; a project that legitimately defaults optional variables will need those sites excluded by path. The other two are literal: a hardcoded host written as an IP other than 127.0.0.1 or 0.0.0.0, a machine name behind a corporate DNS suffix, and a Windows path written with backslashes all match nothing. Values hardcoded as numbers — a port, a retry budget, a timeout — carry no quotes and are invisible to every pattern here. Nothing compares a literal against what the deployed configuration actually uses, which is the only way to know a value is wrong rather than merely inline.

evidence.source: Behavioural class; no rule id claimed because no confirmed ESLint rule bans env-var literal fallbacks.

classes.title: Debug output or breakpoint left in the code
agentModes: Adds console.log tracing while diagnosing and ships it with the fix
Leaves a debugger statement in a browser path, which halts every session with devtools open
Prints request or user objects, quietly turning debug output into a log-privacy incident
classes.gapNotes: A CLI whose entire job is printing to stdout will match constantly, so tool entry points need excluding by path or the class becomes noise. It does not see debug output routed through a real logger at debug level, which is the same information leak with better manners, nor a console call built dynamically as `console['log'](…)`. Severity is hygiene rather than safety, but the log-privacy variant — printing a request or user object — is genuinely a safety problem this class cannot grade.

evidence.source: ESLint core rules no-console (with its allow option) and no-debugger, from the ESLint rules reference.

classes.title: Test or CI step that cannot fail
agentModes: Rewrites the npm test script to echo or exit 0 so `npm test` reports success
Appends `|| true` to a check so the CI job stays green regardless of the result
Adds continue-on-error or --passWithNoTests to a workflow step, then claims the suite passed
classes.gapNotes: --passWithNoTests is legitimate at a monorepo root where some packages genuinely ship no tests, so that pattern needs a per-repo waiver rather than blanket enforcement. It reads only package.json, so a suite neutered inside a Makefile, a turbo.json task or a nested workspace script is missed. It matches the neutering spellings listed and nothing else: a script that pipes the runner into `true`, one that shells out to a wrapper which swallows the exit code, and one that runs the suite under `set +e` are all equally toothless and carry none of these tokens. Nothing here proves the suite actually ran and passed — only a coverage or JUnit artifact published from the run does that, which is a CI-artifact check this lever cannot perform.

evidence.source: Vitest CLI reference documents --passWithNoTests and --allowOnly (default !process.env.CI); npm scripts semantics from the npm CLI docs.

classes.title: CI step neutered so the job stays green
agentModes: Adds continue-on-error to the step whose failure it could not fix
Appends || true to a run line so a red check reports success
Sets if: false on the test step, leaving the workflow looking complete

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4

classes.gapNotes: A regex over YAML, not a parser: `continue-on-error: ${{ inputs.soft }}` and a step disabled through a reusable-workflow input evaluate to the same thing at run time and match nothing. It also cannot see the most effective neutering of all — deleting the step, or removing the workflow's required-check status in branch protection, neither of which leaves a token in the file. The `|| true` pattern is anchored per line, so a continuation written with a YAML block scalar over two lines escapes it.

evidence.source: continue-on-error and if are documented GitHub Actions workflow-syntax keys.

classes.title: Code built from data and executed
agentModes: Reaches for eval or new Function to parse or template something the stdlib already handles
Builds a require path from a variable so a plugin loads by name
Constructs a RegExp from unvalidated input, opening a redos path
classes.gapNotes: The fourth pattern flags every non-literal RegExp, including one built from a vetted constant, which is why that detector's paired rule is marked heuristic. String bodies are blanked, which none of the four patterns needs — the third anchors on the opening quote — and which keeps an `eval(` written inside a quoted code sample or an error message from being reported as a live call. Indirect execution — `globalThis['ev' + 'al'](s)`, `import(dataUrl)`, a worker constructed from a Blob, or `vm.runInNewContext` — matches nothing here. This class does not attempt to judge redos in a literal regex; that is what security/detect-unsafe-regex covers, and it is not wired in above.

evidence.source: ESLint core no-eval and no-implied-eval; security/detect-eval-with-expression and security/detect-non-literal-regexp confirmed in the eslint-plugin-security rule list.

classes.title: Array or record index treated as always present
agentModes: Indexes an array inside a loop bound it derived from a different array
Reads a Map or Record entry and dereferences it without checking for undefined
Destructures a fixed number of elements from a split whose length it never validated
classes.gapNotes: No check-driver detector, because `xs[i].foo` is only a defect when the element type does not already include undefined — a regex cannot know that and would flag every array access in the repo. Both flags are TypeScript-only, so a plain-JS package gets nothing from this class unless allowJs and checkJs are on with JSDoc types. noUncheckedIndexedAccess is also easy to defeat with the non-null assertion this catalogue flags separately.

evidence.source: noUncheckedIndexedAccess and noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature confirmed in the TypeScript TSConfig reference.

classes.title: Loose equality where coercion changes the answer
agentModes: Switches === to == after a comparison between a string and a number fails
Writes == null deliberately in one place and == elsewhere by imitation of that line
classes.gapNotes: The lookbehind excludes ===, !==, >=, <= and compound assignment, but any arrow function written `=>` is unaffected only because it is a single `=`; a fat-arrow typo `==>` would match. The rule's smart/allow-null options make `== null` legal in many codebases, and the regex has no such exemption, so a project that uses `x == null` idiomatically will need it excluded. Coercion bugs that use `===` on values already coerced upstream by `+` or template interpolation are outside this class entirely.

evidence.source: ESLint core rule eqeqeq and its 'always' option, from the ESLint rules reference.

classes.title: Fewer test cases after the edit than before it
agentModes: Deletes the failing test case and reports the suite green
Trims a parameterised case list down to the inputs that already pass
Removes the whole case rather than the assertion inside it, so no empty test body is left to find
classes.gapNotes: A removal is not in any file's content — the deleted case is absent from the file that is left, so a pathless check-driver run reports this class skipped and proves it only from the fixture pair, which carries the file before the edit and the file after it. The commit lane is the run that holds both versions: `--staged` counts the index against HEAD, a file deleted outright included, so a commit that shrinks the suite is a finding there. The earlier lane is an authored `edit-guard` on the same removal rule — a catalogue never carries a session guard, so that half is the owner's to author. It reads one edit at a time: an Edit payload carries the text it replaced, so a case deleted out of a `describe` block is seen, and a Write payload carries none, so a whole-file rewrite that drops a spec file is not. Author it to observe: one call cannot see the case being put back two calls later, and a deletion can be right — behaviour that genuinely went away takes its tests with it, which is a judgement no count can make.

evidence.source: No tool in the JavaScript and TypeScript ecosystem gates on a drop in test count between two revisions; the runners report what they discovered, never what they stopped discovering. The judgement that a shrinking suite is a defect is jig's own.

classes.title: Stub left throwing while the task is reported done
agentModes: Leaves `throw new Error('not implemented')` in a function whose signature and call sites it already wrote
Marks the missing half with a TODO comment and reports the change complete
Returns an empty array or null from a function it did not write, so callers type-check and the suite passes vacuously
classes.gapNotes: Both tokens are also the correct code somewhere, so what is reported is a guess about intent rather than a fact about the source: `throw new Error('not implemented')` is the right body for an abstract base method, and a TODO comment is often a note about a later improvement sitting over finished code. The first detector reads string bodies, which is the only way to see the message, so it is the one detector in this edition that runs with stripStrings off — a message assembled from a variable is invisible to it. The quietest form of the mistake has no token at all: a function that returns `null`, `[]` or `0` because the session did not know what to compute, which only a test asserting the real value catches. The near miss carries the traps — `TODO_REVIEW_LIMIT` and `todoItems()` are code, not comments, and a genuine `throw new Error` whose message is not a stub token must stay silent.

evidence.source: No ESLint rule in the config jig installs reports a stub: `no-warning-comments` exists in ESLint core but is off by default and is not in the shipped flat config, so no tool-rule detector is claimed here.

classes.title: Timer standing in for a real wait condition in a test
agentModes: Adds a setTimeout sleep to make an intermittently failing async test pass on the machine it is running on
Increases an existing sleep when the test fails again, rather than waiting on the condition
Sleeps because it does not know which awaiting primitive or fake-timer helper the project already has
classes.gapNotes: The call site is matched exactly, but whether the call is a defect is not decidable from the text: a sleep is correct when the test is deliberately exercising timing, which makes this a project-policy class whose value comes from the ledger rather than the match. No ESLint rule in the shipped config bans it, and none honestly could, so there is no tool-rule detector. It reads two spellings and no more — a bare `setTimeout(done, 500)` in a callback-style test, a project helper named `wait` or `delay` rather than `sleep`, and `vi.advanceTimersByTime` used without any fake timers installed all carry neither token. The near miss holds the trap: a method named `sleepBudgetMillis` mentions sleeping without doing it.

evidence.source: setTimeout is a documented Web/Node timer API and the promise-wrapped form is the ordinary JavaScript sleep idiom; the judgement that it is a synchronisation smell inside a test is jig's own policy, backed by no rule id — hence the missing tool-rule detector.

classes.title: Test harness config relaxed instead of the failure fixed
agentModes: Lowers the coverage threshold to whatever the current run happens to reach, then reports the suite green
Flips the switch that makes a focused or empty run fail, so a narrowed suite stops being an error
Edits the harness config jig installed rather than the code that made it fail
classes.gapNotes: The near miss is the vitest.config.ts jig writes, character for character, so this class fails the moment it would fire on jig's own install. It reads values, never a diff: a threshold moved from 80 to 55 is a real loosening and matches nothing here, because only a single-digit threshold is distinguishable from a project that never set one high. It also cannot see the loosening that leaves no value at all — the `thresholds` block deleted, the coverage provider removed, or the whole config file replaced by a smaller one. Scoped to the vitest and vite config files, so a threshold carried in package.json or passed on the command line is out of its reach, and `--coverage.thresholds.lines=0` on a CI run line is invisible to it.

evidence.source: allowOnly, passWithNoTests, coverage.enabled and coverage.thresholds are all documented keys of the Vitest configuration reference; the near miss is jig's own installed configSample for this edition.

classes.title: Snapshots regenerated by a committed command instead of reviewed
agentModes: Commits a script or CI step that runs the test suite with the snapshot-update flag, so every failing snapshot is rewritten to whatever the code now produces
Adds the update flag to the standing test command after a snapshot diff it could not explain
Leaves a workflow step that refreshes snapshots on every run, which makes the snapshot suite incapable of failing

fixtures.violation:
name: verify
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run -u
fixtures.nearMiss:
name: verify
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run --coverage
      - run: npm test -- --reporter=github-actions

classes.gapNotes: This reads what was COMMITTED and nothing else: a session that types `npx vitest -u` in a terminal leaves no file to match, and catching that would need a session guard, which a catalogue never carries — the owner authors it. Two runners are named, so a snapshot updater under another name (ava, ember, a project wrapper script) is missed, as is the environment-variable spelling `CI=false` that makes some runners write snapshots by default. It cannot tell a deliberate, reviewed regeneration from a blind one; the committed flag is the evidence, not the verdict.

evidence.source: `-u, --update` is documented in the Vitest CLI reference and `-u, --updateSnapshot` in the Jest CLI reference; both rewrite every failing snapshot in the run.
